definitionAnchor.quote: the price where the quantity demanded by buyers equals the quantity supplied by sellers

mcItems.q: Researchers observe two groups after a policy change and want to claim the policy caused the difference. What condition is required for that causal interpretation?
op: The groups must be comparable apart from the change.
The groups must be perfectly identical in every respect.
Any two groups are enough if the sample is large.
A causal claim is justified whenever the data are observational.
mcItems.ex: Correct: the causal claim is credible only if the groups were comparable apart from the change. The common misconception is that large observational samples alone establish causation; size cannot replace comparability, because a confounding factor could still explain the difference.

keyTerms.df: A design that uses an outside change to compare one affected group with another unaffected group.

mcItems.q: A household saves part of its income instead of spending it on domestically produced goods and services. In the circular flow, what is that saving best described as?
op: A leakage that reduces spending in the flow
A government injection that adds spending to the flow
An export that returns money to firms
A price change that shifts equilibrium
mcItems.ex: Correct: saving is a leakage because money earned by households does not keep circulating as spending unless it is returned through some other channel. The most plausible mistake is to treat saving like an injection, but injections are additions such as investment, government spending, and exports.

mcItems.q: In a simplified economy, total leakages from the circular flow are exactly matched by total injections. What follows from that balance?
op: National income neither rises nor falls
Household income must fall because saving is high
Imports must equal exports in every market
Firms will always earn zero profit
mcItems.ex: Correct: when leakages equal injections, the circular flow is in balance and national income neither rises nor falls. The tempting misconception is to read balance as a statement about fairness, profits, or trade in every market, but the source claim is only about the income flow staying steady.

keyTerms.df: A withdrawal from the spending stream that stops money from continuing to circulate through firms.
keyTerms.eg: A household sets aside part of its income as saving rather than buying output.
keyTerms.mi: Any money leaving a household must be a tax.
keyTerms.cx: Some withdrawals are saving, some are taxes, and some are spending on imports; all are leakages in this model.

keyTerms.df: An addition to the spending stream that puts money back into circulation.
keyTerms.eg: Government spending on infrastructure adds demand to firms' sales.
keyTerms.mi: Only private investment counts as an injection.
keyTerms.cx: The model names investment, government spending, and exports as injections, so public spending and exports also qualify.

mcItems.q: A factory buys new machines during the year, while some older equipment wears out. According to the source, which statement best describes the change in its capital stock over that period?
op: It changes by net investment, which equals gross investment minus depreciation.
It always rises whenever any new machine is purchased.
It rises only when depreciation is exactly zero.
It is unchanged unless output also increases.
mcItems.ex: Correct: net investment is the change in the capital stock over a period. Misconception: any new purchase does not by itself determine the change, because depreciation must also be counted.

mcItems.q: Which condition is required for an economy’s capital stock to grow over time, based on the source?
op: Net investment must be positive.
Gross investment must be larger than output.
Depreciation must be positive.
The number of tools must stay fixed.
mcItems.ex: Correct: the capital stock grows only when net investment is positive. Misconception: positive gross investment alone is not enough if depreciation is larger.

keyTerms.df: The total amount of productive equipment, structures, and tools available for production.
keyTerms.eg: A firm’s machines, buildings, and other tools used in making goods count toward its capital stock.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same thing as annual investment spending.
keyTerms.cx: Investment spending can add to capital stock, but the stock itself is the accumulated quantity on hand.

keyTerms.df: The amount left after depreciation is subtracted from gross investment; it shows the period-to-period change in capital stock.
keyTerms.eg: If a business buys new equipment but some old equipment wears out, the remaining increase after wear and tear is net investment.
keyTerms.mi: It is identical to gross investment.
keyTerms.cx: Gross investment becomes net investment only after depreciation is accounted for.

mcItems.q: What is a proxy variable?
op: An observable stand-in used to measure something that cannot be observed directly
A direct measurement of the target construct itself
A policy rule that changes prices over time
A random error that makes data unusable
mcItems.ex: It is an observable stand-in for an unobserved construct. It is not the construct itself.

keyTerms.df: An observable stand-in used to measure something that cannot be seen directly.
keyTerms.eg: A city may use GDP as a stand-in for economic well-being when the broader idea itself is not directly observable.
keyTerms.mi: A proxy variable is the same thing as the hidden construct it represents.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that a proxy is only a measure of the construct, so it can miss important parts of what it is meant to summarize.

keyTerms.df: A measure of marketed output that is often used as a stand-in for economic well-being.
keyTerms.eg: A policy memo might cite GDP when comparing two countries’ apparent prosperity.
keyTerms.mi: GDP fully captures well-being because it is a large economic number.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that GDP misses unpaid work, income distribution, and environmental costs, so it should not be treated as the full construct of well-being.

mcItems.q: A worker stops searching after many rejected applications. Under the labor-force boundary described in the source, how is that person counted?
op: Unemployed, because the person still wants a job.
Out of the labor force, because the person has given up looking.
Employed, because the person once searched for work.
The evidence is too limited to classify the person.
mcItems.ex: Correct: the person is counted out of the labor force. The common misconception is to treat giving up the search as unemployment, but the source says people who have given up looking are not classified as unemployed.

mcItems.q: A change in how the labor-force boundary is drawn affects the reported jobless figure. What does the source say happens to the measured unemployment rate?
op: It stays fixed because the label does not matter.
It changes when the boundary is redrawn.
It only changes if wages also change.
The evidence does not support any measurement effect.
mcItems.ex: Correct: the measured unemployment rate changes when the boundary is drawn differently. The tempting misconception is that the rate is purely objective and unaffected by classification choices, but the source directly says the boundary changes the measurement.

keyTerms.df: A person who wants work but has stopped searching, so the count can exclude that person from unemployment.
keyTerms.eg: After repeated job rejections, a job seeker quits looking and is no longer counted as unemployed in the source’s classification.
keyTerms.mi: If someone wants a job, they must still be counted as unemployed.
keyTerms.cx: The source says giving up the search places the person out of the labor force, not unemployed, and that exclusion can make unemployment look lower than the felt experience of joblessness.

keyTerms.df: The rule set used to sort people into labor-market categories such as unemployed or out of the labor force.
keyTerms.eg: A survey boundary treats a person who has stopped looking for work as outside the labor force rather than unemployed.
keyTerms.mi: It is just another name for the unemployment rate itself.
keyTerms.cx: Classification is the method that produces the measured rate; the rate is the result, not the rule set.

mcItems.q: A student skips a paid movie night to study in the library, using time and energy they could have spent elsewhere. What is the opportunity cost of studying?
op: The value of the next best alternative given up
The ticket price of the movie she did not buy
The total money spent on textbooks this week
The usefulness of studying compared with relaxing
mcItems.ex: Correct: opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone, here the movie night or any other best use of that time and energy. Misconception: the ticket price is a cash expense, but the concept also includes time and other resources that could have produced something else.

mcItems.q: A commuter says, “Riding my own bike costs nothing because I do not pay a fare.” Which response best applies the opportunity-cost idea?
op: It may still have an opportunity cost if the time could be used elsewhere
It has no cost unless cash changes hands
Its cost is exactly the fare for a bus
It is free whenever the bike was already owned
mcItems.ex: Correct: even when no money is paid, using time or resources can still forgo something else, so the choice can have opportunity cost. Misconception: treating only cash payments as cost ignores the next best alternative that is given up.

keyTerms.df: The value of the best alternative given up when a choice is made.
keyTerms.eg: Choosing to study for an exam instead of working an extra hour means the forgone work time is part of the cost.
keyTerms.mi: It is only the cash paid for the item chosen.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that time and other resources can matter even when no money changes hands.

keyTerms.df: The most valuable option that remains unavailable after a decision uses time or resources.
keyTerms.eg: Spending Saturday afternoon on homework means the next best alternative might have been part-time work or another planned activity.
keyTerms.mi: It means every skipped option, all at once.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is to focus on the single best forgone alternative, not the entire list of missed possibilities.
